problems.statement:
There was a monitoring of a bright star in Mumbai over a whole night. It has been done with a 14" telescope in three wavelength bands (B, V and R bands). Assume that the observed wavelengths can be approximated by effective wavelengths of 450 nm, 550 nm and 700 nm for the observed star. As the night progresses, the star is seen at different zenith angles and hence the starlight passes through different thickness of the Earth's atmosphere. Consequently, the extinction due to the Earth's atmosphere changes; it is minimum when the star is closest to the zenith and maximum when the star is rising or setting. Sample data are given in the table. The air-mass in the second column gives effective air-mass of the atmosphere normalized with the air mass at zero zenith angle taken as one. Magnitudes are correct to $0.05^m$.

| Zenith Angle (deg) | Air-mass | B magnitude | V magnitude | R magnitude |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 15 | 1.035 | 2.80 | 0.85 | -1.00 |
| 30 | 1.154 | 2.85 | 0.85 | -1.00 |
| 45 | 1.412 | 3.00 | 0.95 | -0.90 |
| 60 | 1.991 | 3.20 | 1.10 | -0.85 |
| 69 | 2.762 | 3.50 | 1.30 | -0.75 |
| 75 | 3.785 | 3.90 | 1.55 | -0.55 |
| 81 | 6.053 | 4.90 | 2.15 | -0.25 |
problems.title: Monitoring of a star.

parts.statement: Plot the appropriate graph and find the apparent magnitude of the star in the three wavelengths, in the absence of Earth's atmosphere.

The Hipparcos satellite gave a parallax of 0.0076 arcseconds for this star. Mark the location of the star in the H-R Diagram given separately.

![](p6-hr)

figures.alt: Original Hertzsprung-Russell diagram with spectral classes and absolute magnitudes.

parts.statement:
The colour index can be calibrated in terms of the stellar temperature. An empirical fit (for the region of H-R diagram to which this star belongs) is given by:

$$B-V=-3.68\log(T)+14.55$$

(where T is the absolute temperature).

Estimate the temperature of the star.

If the particular star was in the constellation Orion, which is the most likely candidate out of the four brightest stars in the constellation? Write the Latin name of the star (you have to write in roman script, spelling mistakes will be tolerated as long as the name of the star is understandable).
In Mumbai, let us assume the extinction varies as $\lambda^{-\alpha}$ (where $\lambda$ is the wavelength). From the given data, find parameter $\alpha$.

solution.incompleteReason: No solution for this problem is supplied in the complete 2006 archive. The available practsol.xls contains only the period-data table and plotted curve for Group beta problem 7.1.

problems.statement:
A radio pulsar is a rapidly spinning neutron star emitting beams of radio waves from its magnetic poles. These are observed on Earth as series of pulses separated by the apparent pulse period $P_t$. When the pulsar is a member of a binary system, this differs from the true pulse period ($P_0$) of the pulsar. The pulsar 0514-40 was studied with the GMRT, India in the year 2004. The true pulse period of this pulsar is $P_0=4.990575$ ms.

Table gives data of $P_t$ as a function of time in units of orbital period, $t/T$ ($T=18.35$ days). Assume the observer is located in the orbital plane of the pulsar.
problems.title: A Binary Radio Pulsar.

parts.statement: Make a graph of this data set (scale the graph properly).
If the orbit had been circular, shape of the data curve would not be the same as the graph you have just drawn. Sketch the shape of the data curve for a circular orbit.
parts.statementAfter:
A graph of the elliptical orbit of the pulsar with eccentricity 0.866 is provided to you (for the pulsar 0514-40, the eccentricity of orbit is very close to this value). The arrow on the curve indicates the pulsar is moving anticlockwise in its orbit around the focus O. AP and BD are perpendicular to each other; AP is the major axis of the ellipse.

![](p7-orbit-grid)

figures.alt: Original elliptical orbit on graph paper, focus, labelled axes and tangent at B.

parts.statement: Taking $u_A$ at A as unit speed, calculate the transverse speeds at positions B, P and D (transverse speed $u_G$ of the pulsar at any point G is the magnitude of the component perpendicular to OG).

On the graph of orbit provided to you, a tangent to the curve at point B is shown on the graph. Using the graph of the orbit or otherwise, determine the total speed at B, P and D ($v_B$, $v_P$ and $v_D$ respectively) in the same unit of speed.
From the shape of the $P_t$ versus $t/T$ data, infer whether the observer is located close to the major axis, or minor axis of the orbit and on which side.
Assume that the velocity component parallel to the major axis is maximum at the points B and D. Mark the points A, B, P and D on the graph of the data drawn by you.
Sketch roughly, on the same graph paper, the $P_t$ vs. $t/T$ curve if the observer was on the axis perpendicular to that in 7.5.
From the orbital graph, estimate the fraction of the total orbital period taken to travel the arc DPB. Estimate the same from the graph of the data you have drawn.

Draw a line $P_t=P_0$ on your graph of the data. Measure the areas under the curve you have drawn on the upper and lower sides of this line and use it to give an estimate of the major axis in light seconds.

figures.alt: Original schematic ellipse with A, B, P, D, focus O, G and direction arrows.
